title: Continuity and Types of Discontinuity
subject: AP Calculus AB
objectives: State and apply the three-part definition of continuity at a point to determine whether a function is continuous there
Classify discontinuities as removable, jump, or infinite by analyzing one-sided limits and function values
Determine whether a function is continuous over an interval and identify the functions that are continuous on their domains
Determine values of a parameter that make a piecewise-defined function continuous (removing a discontinuity)

sections.heading: The Three Conditions for Continuity
sections.content:
You've probably heard the informal definition: a function is continuous if you can draw its graph 'without lifting your pencil.' That's a decent first intuition, but for calculus you need the precise definition. A function f is continuous at a point x = a if and only if three conditions are ALL met:

1. f(a) is defined — the function actually has a value at x = a. There's a filled-in dot on the graph, not a hole.

2. lim(x→a) f(x) exists — the function approaches a single value as x gets close to a from both sides. The left-hand limit and right-hand limit must agree.

3. lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a) — the value the function approaches actually equals the value the function takes. The limit and the function value match.

Think of it as a three-part handshake. The function has to show up (condition 1), the limit has to show up (condition 2), and they have to agree on the same number (condition 3). If any one of these fails, the function is discontinuous at that point.

Here's an analogy: imagine you're meeting a friend at a restaurant. Condition 1 is that you actually go to the restaurant (you exist there). Condition 2 is that your friend is heading to the same restaurant from their direction (they're approaching). Condition 3 is that you're both at the *same* restaurant (you agree on the location). If any of these breaks down — you don't show up, they can't decide which restaurant, or you go to different places — the meetup fails.

Notice that condition 3 is secretly the strongest one: if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a) is true, then automatically f(a) must be defined and the limit must exist, because you can't have an equation between things that don't exist. That's why many textbooks state continuity in the single compact line 'lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).' But on the AP exam, checking all three conditions explicitly keeps you from missing a case.

sections.heading: How to Test Continuity at a Point x = a

steps.title: Check that f(a) is defined
steps.content: Find the actual function value at x = a. For a piecewise function, use the rule that explicitly covers x = a. If the function has no value there (a hole, or division by zero), it is already discontinuous — stop.

steps.title: Find the left-hand limit
steps.content: Compute lim(x→a⁻) f(x) using the piece of the function that applies just below a. This is the value the curve heads toward from the left.

steps.title: Find the right-hand limit
steps.content: Compute lim(x→a⁺) f(x) using the piece that applies just above a. If the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist and the function is discontinuous — stop.

steps.title: Confirm the limit equals the function value
steps.content: If the two one-sided limits agree on a value L, then lim(x→a) f(x) = L. Check whether L equals f(a). If they match, f is continuous at a; if not, it is discontinuous there.

sections.heading: Testing Continuity at a Point
sections.content:
Consider the piecewise function:
  f(x) = x² + 1   when x < 2
  f(x) = 5          when x = 2
  f(x) = 4x - 3    when x > 2

Is f continuous at x = 2?

Condition 1: Is f(2) defined? Yes — the middle piece tells us f(2) = 5. ✓

Condition 2: Does lim(x→2) f(x) exist?
  Left-hand limit: lim(x→2⁻) (x² + 1) = 4 + 1 = 5.
  Right-hand limit: lim(x→2⁺) (4x - 3) = 8 - 3 = 5.
  Both sides give 5, so the two-sided limit exists and equals 5. ✓

Condition 3: Does lim(x→2) f(x) = f(2)? The limit is 5 and f(2) = 5. Yes! ✓

All three conditions pass, so f is continuous at x = 2.

Now change the middle piece to f(2) = 7. Conditions 1 and 2 still pass (f(2) = 7 is defined, and the limit is still 5). But condition 3 fails: the limit (5) doesn't equal f(2) (7). Now f is discontinuous at x = 2 — specifically a removable discontinuity, since the limit exists but the value is 'misplaced.'

sections.question: A function h satisfies lim(x→4⁻) h(x) = 6, lim(x→4⁺) h(x) = 6, and h(4) = 6. A second function k satisfies lim(x→4⁻) k(x) = 6, lim(x→4⁺) k(x) = 6, but k(4) is undefined. Which functions are continuous at x = 4?
options: Both h and k, because their limits exist and equal 6
Only h, because k fails condition 1 (k(4) is not defined)
Only k, because the limit is what matters
Neither, because a limit of 6 is not enough
sections.explanation: Continuity requires all three conditions. h passes all three. k has a perfectly good limit of 6, but k(4) is undefined, so it fails condition 1 — k has a removable discontinuity at x = 4. An existing limit alone is not enough; the function value must exist and match.

sections.heading: Three Types of Discontinuity
sections.content:
When continuity fails, it fails in one of three characteristic ways. Learning to recognize each type is important for the AP exam and for building your mathematical intuition.

**Removable Discontinuity (the 'hole'):** This happens when the limit exists but either f(a) is undefined or f(a) doesn't match the limit. On a graph, it looks like a single missing point — a hole in the curve, possibly with a stray dot plotted somewhere else. It's called 'removable' because you could fix it by redefining f(a) to equal the limit. Think of it like a single missing tile on a floor — the pattern is clear, and you could fill in the gap. Example: f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x - 2) has a removable discontinuity at x = 2 because the function simplifies to x + 2 everywhere except x = 2, where it's undefined. The limit is 4, but f(2) doesn't exist.

**Jump Discontinuity:** This occurs when both one-sided limits exist but they aren't equal. On a graph, the function literally 'jumps' from one value to another — there's a clean break. Think of a staircase: at each step, the height suddenly changes. Tax brackets work this way too — your marginal rate 'jumps' as you cross income thresholds. Example: the greatest integer (floor) function has jump discontinuities at every integer; at x = 3 it jumps from 2 (from the left) to 3 (from the right).

**Infinite Discontinuity:** This happens when at least one of the one-sided limits is ±∞. The function blows up near the point, creating a vertical asymptote. On a graph, you see the curve shooting up or down toward infinity. Example: f(x) = 1/x has an infinite discontinuity at x = 0 — as x → 0⁺, f(x) → +∞, and as x → 0⁻, f(x) → -∞.

A single hole (open circle), maybe a stray dot

sections.heading: Classifying Discontinuities
sections.content:
For each function, identify the type of discontinuity:

1) f(x) = (x² - x - 6)/(x - 3) at x = 3.
Factor numerator: (x - 3)(x + 2)/(x - 3). After canceling: x + 2. The limit as x → 3 is 5, but f(3) is undefined. The limit exists, so this is a REMOVABLE discontinuity.

2) g(x) = { x + 1 if x < 1; 2x - 3 if x ≥ 1 } at x = 1.
Left limit: lim(x→1⁻) (x + 1) = 2. Right limit: lim(x→1⁺) (2x - 3) = -1. Since 2 ≠ -1, this is a JUMP discontinuity.

3) h(x) = 1/(x - 4)² at x = 4.
As x → 4 from either side, (x - 4)² → 0⁺ (always positive), so h(x) → +∞. This is an INFINITE discontinuity (vertical asymptote at x = 4).

Quick classification rule: if the limit exists (but doesn't match the function value or the value is missing), it's removable. If the one-sided limits exist but disagree, it's a jump. If any one-sided limit is ±∞, it's infinite.

sections.question: The function f(x) = (x - 5)/(x² - 25) is undefined at both x = 5 and x = -5. What kinds of discontinuities are these?
options: x = 5 is removable; x = -5 is infinite
x = 5 is infinite; x = -5 is removable
sections.explanation: Factor: (x - 5)/[(x - 5)(x + 5)] = 1/(x + 5) for x ≠ 5. At x = 5 the (x - 5) cancels, leaving a finite limit of 1/10 — a hole, so removable. At x = -5 nothing cancels and the denominator → 0 with a nonzero numerator, so the function blows up — infinite. Not every 'undefined' point is the same type.

sections.content: Continuity at x = a requires three things: (1) f(a) is defined, (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists, (3) they are equal. The three failure modes are removable (limit exists, hole), jump (one-sided limits disagree), and infinite (a one-sided limit is ±∞).

sections.heading: Which Functions Are Continuous Where
sections.content: Memorize these so you can spot discontinuities instantly: polynomials are continuous for ALL real numbers; rational functions are continuous everywhere EXCEPT where the denominator is zero; √x is continuous for x ≥ 0; sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere; eˣ is continuous everywhere; ln x is continuous for x > 0; tan x is discontinuous where cos x = 0. A function built by adding, multiplying, or composing continuous functions is continuous wherever all the pieces are.

sections.heading: Continuity on an Interval and Removing Discontinuities
sections.content:
So far we've checked continuity at single points. A function is *continuous on an interval* if it's continuous at every point in that interval. For a closed interval [a, b], the endpoints only need one-sided continuity: at the left endpoint a we require lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = f(a), and at the right endpoint b we require lim(x→b⁻) f(x) = f(b). This matters because the big theorems coming later — the Extreme Value Theorem, the Intermediate Value Theorem — all require continuity on a closed interval as their entry ticket.

Now here's a skill the AP exam absolutely loves: *removing a discontinuity* by choosing a parameter. Suppose a piecewise function has an unknown constant k, and you're asked to find the value of k that makes the function continuous. The strategy is always the same — force the pieces to agree at the boundary. You set the left-hand limit equal to the right-hand limit equal to the function value at the seam, then solve for k.

Why does this work? A piecewise function can only break at the seams where the rule changes; within each piece it's usually a polynomial or other continuous function, so it's automatically continuous there. So the only place trouble can happen is at the boundary points, and continuity at a boundary is exactly the equation 'left limit = right limit = value.' Solving that equation for the unknown welds the two pieces together with no gap and no jump.

This is the engine behind the next lesson too: when a rational function has a removable discontinuity (a hole), you can 'patch' it by defining the missing value to equal the limit — that's removing the discontinuity in action.

sections.heading: Finding the Constant That Makes a Function Continuous
sections.content:
Find the value of k that makes the following function continuous everywhere:
  f(x) = x² + k   when x ≤ 3
  f(x) = 2x + 1    when x > 3

Step 1: Identify where trouble could occur. Each piece is a polynomial, so each is continuous on its own. The only possible break is at the seam x = 3, where the rule changes.

Step 2: Write the continuity condition at x = 3 — the left piece's value must equal the right piece's limit:
  Left value / left limit: f(3) = 3² + k = 9 + k.
  Right-hand limit: lim(x→3⁺) (2x + 1) = 2(3) + 1 = 7.

Step 3: Set them equal and solve for k:
  9 + k = 7
  k = -2.

Step 4: Interpret. With k = -2, the left piece gives f(3) = 9 + (-2) = 7, matching the right-hand limit of 7. The two pieces meet at the point (3, 7) with no gap and no jump, so f is continuous everywhere. Any other value of k would leave a jump discontinuity at x = 3.

sections.heading: Watch the Boundary Inequalities and Use Every Condition
sections.content: Two traps on continuity problems. First, when a piecewise function asks for a parameter, the equation you solve is left-limit = right-limit at the seam — students often plug into only one piece and forget to match the other. Second, if a problem gives TWO unknown constants (say it must be continuous AND differentiable), one continuity equation isn't enough — you need a second equation from matching derivatives. Always count your unknowns and make sure you have that many equations before solving.

sections.heading: Why Continuity Matters Beyond This Chapter
sections.content:
You might be tempted to think of continuity as a topic you learn once and move past. But continuity is actually a recurring character throughout all of AP Calculus, showing up in crucial moments when you least expect it.

The most important connection: differentiability requires continuity. If a function is differentiable at a point (meaning it has a derivative there — a well-defined slope), then it MUST be continuous at that point. The reverse isn't true — a function can be continuous but not differentiable (like the absolute value function at x = 0, which is continuous but has a sharp corner). But a discontinuous function is NEVER differentiable at the discontinuity. So every time you take a derivative, you're implicitly relying on continuity. You'll explore this two-way relationship in detail in Unit 2.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — the crown jewel of the course — has continuity as a hypothesis. It says that if f is continuous on [a, b], then the definite integral from a to b of f(x) dx exists and can be computed using antiderivatives. Without continuity, the whole bridge between derivatives and integrals could collapse.

The Intermediate Value Theorem (the very next lesson) and the Extreme Value Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem (Unit 5) all open with the same hypothesis: 'Let f be continuous on the closed interval [a, b].' These theorems are what let you guarantee solutions exist, that maximums and minimums exist, and that average rates are achieved instantaneously. Every one of them is unlocked by the single key of continuity.

So when you verify continuity on the AP exam, you're not just checking a box — you're confirming that the powerful machinery of calculus is allowed to operate. It's like checking that the bridge is intact before you drive across it.

aiContext: This is Unit 1 Lesson 3 of AP Calculus AB. Emphasize the three-part definition and have students check all three conditions explicitly rather than eyeballing the graph. The biggest sources of confusion: (1) thinking an existing limit alone means continuity (they forget the value must be defined AND match), and (2) misclassifying discontinuities — especially treating every 'undefined' point as the same type when factoring reveals some are removable holes and others are infinite asymptotes. The 'find k to make f continuous' problem is heavily tested; guide students to set left-limit = right-limit at the seam and to count unknowns versus equations (continuity gives one equation; adding differentiability gives a second). Connect forward: continuity is the hypothesis for the IVT (next lesson), the EVT and MVT (Unit 5), and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Unit 6), and it is necessary for differentiability (Unit 2). On the AP exam this shows up as multiple-choice classification of discontinuities and as free-response parts asking students to justify continuity or solve for a parameter.
